html:
A Hindu temple to Shiva at Ellora in Maharashtra, India, carved downward and inward out of a single basalt hillside in the 8th century. It is usually credited to the Rashtrakuta king Krishna I.

The builders did not stack stones. They cut three deep trenches into the slope and then carved the whole temple from the block left in the middle: shrine, hall, gateway, pillars, life-size stone elephants and a bridge. Some 200,000 tonnes of rock are thought to have been removed. The design copies a free-standing temple, and was meant to recall Mount Kailash, Shiva's home in the Himalayas.

Ellora has 34 caves made by Buddhists, Hindus and Jains over about five centuries, side by side. The Kailasa is the largest and the boldest. Like the earlier Ajanta caves nearby, it shows how far rock-cut building went in India. Ellora is a World Heritage Site.
